key_numbers.value: Adult care home (ACH) = 7+ residents, licensed under 10A NCAC 13F; family care home (FCH) = 2–6 residents, licensed under 10A NCAC 13G; both under G.S. Chapter 131D [S1][S2][S5]

No new adult care home beds may be developed without a CON. Applications are accepted only for counties with a scheduled review. DHSR decides within 150 days of the start of the review period. CON must be satisfied before the license application [S1][S3]. Whether CON applies to 2–6 bed family care homes was not verified.

key_numbers.metric: Initial license fee — adult care home (7+)
key_numbers.value: DHSR licensing page: $400 non-refundable + $19 per bed, paid with the application [S1][S7]. This conflicts with the G.S. 131D-2.5 schedule on DHSR forms ($360 + $17.50 per bed annual) [S6]. Unresolved; the model should use the higher DHSR-page figure.
ACH: $360 + $17.50 per bed, invoiced by ACLS [S1]. FCH: $315 [S2][S6]. FCH initial licensure fee: $350 [S2].
key_numbers.as_of: ACH page undated; FCH page modified 2025-11-20

key_numbers.value: Initial licenses are issued for 6 months, then ACLS must survey. For FCHs the survey occurs about 4 months after the initial license [S1][S2]. ACLS notifies the applicant and county DSS of its decision within 14 days [S3].

Age 21+; 120-hour Administrator-in-Training (min. 20 hrs coursework + 100 hrs on-the-job); exam fee $50; $30 renewal; 30 CE hrs every 2 years after first renewal. SBI check $14, or $38 with FBI [S8]. FCH administrator approval has no renewal fee [S8].

7–20 residents: at least one designated staff per shift for personal care and supervision; 7–12 residents: administrator or manager on site or within 500 ft with two-way communication; 21–40 residents: 16 aide hours on shifts 1 and 2; 31+: Personal Care Aide Supervisor; 81+: administrator on duty 8 hrs/day, 5 days/week [S9]. Staff with CPR/choking training within 24 months must be on premises at all times [S12].

Special care unit (dementia): $1,792/month; Enhanced Maintenance $1,862 including the $70 personal needs allowance [S29][S30]. Regular ACH: $1,397/month per a secondary guide [S35]; the official SA-In-Home basic rate is also $1,397 [S31]. Funded 50% state / 50% county [S32]. SA recipients are automatically Medicaid-eligible [S32].

key_numbers.metric: Medicaid State Plan PCS rate (HCPCS 99509, HA/HB)
key_numbers.value: $7.03 per unit, up from $5.96 (+18%), effective 2026-08-01. Funded by $70.8M recurring state funds in S.L. 2026-41 / SB 257 §9E.15. Whether ACHs bill this code is unverified [S23].

$6,496/month ($77,955/yr) per CareScout 2025 (provider-reported, collected Jul–Nov 2025, published Mar 2026), secondary summary. National median $6,200/month [S44][S45]. Older Genworth 2024 NC figure of $5,769 is not comparable [S46].
More than 1,200 adult care homes in North Carolina. DHSR publishes separate ACH and FCH listings, updated 07/30/2026 [S16][S17]. The count of family care homes and of licensed beds was not extracted.

65+: 2,038,854 (18%) in 2025, projected 2,996,376 (21%) in 2050 (+47%). 85+: 186,398 in 2025, projected 509,848 in 2050 (+174%). About 211,000 people 65+ projected to live with Alzheimer's in 2025 [S62].

Certificate of Need application fee and the 2026/2027 review schedule. Insurance or bond requirements for ACHs and FCHs — none found in the DHSR pages or rules reviewed. Any premium in the model is an operator estimate (verify locally).

Family care home administrator requirements are verified: high school diploma/GED, a State-approved 120-hour AIT program, the Administrator Exam, age 21+ and an SBI (and FBI if applicable) check. The AIT program cost and the background-check rules for owners, principals and affiliates were not verified.
Local zoning and siting rules (distance, density, use classification) beyond the requirement for local zoning approval, and city/county business-license fees in Charlotte, Raleigh or Greensboro.

Statewide licensed ACH bed totals in 2026, occupancy rates, and counts of licensed ACHs/FCHs by name, county or bed count. The XLSX listings exist [S17] but were not parsed. A 2010-era bed figure was seen and is outdated, so it is not used.
Competitor names, market shares, and referral-source shares (hospital discharge, DSS, family) for ACHs — no public source found.

Special Assistance caseload counts for ACH residents, and any waitlist counts for SA, ACH admission or FCH placement — none found in official sources. A consumer guide says SA In-Home has had no waitlist since the 2021 slot-cap removal [S35]; this is not verified on a primary page.

The regular-ACH SA room-and-board maximum of $1,397 comes from a secondary guide [S35]. It matches the official SA-In-Home basic rate [S31], which the SA-In-Home manual caps at 100% of the SA facility payment [S34]. The ACH-specific official table was not retrieved.

How Medicaid personal care services are billed for ACH residents (separate code, modifier or per-diem arrangement), PCS utilization in ACHs, and the fee-for-service vs managed-care routing — not confirmed. The 99509 HA/HB rate in this report is the published State Plan PCS rate [S23], not a verified ACH billing rate.
The October 2026 'Medicaid Rates Revised FY27' bulletin and the Innovations waiver unit-rate change — contents not verified.
EVV applicability to ACHs: NC Medicaid's EVV scope is in-home PCS [S25]. The statement that ACHs are exempt comes only from a vendor page [S27] and is unconfirmed on NC Medicaid pages.

Official NC Medicaid enrollment fee by provider type and the 'lite' vs full enrollment option — only a vendor source was found [S43]. The $100 NC application fee [S41][S42] and the federal CY2026 $750 institutional fee [S40] are verified; which apply to an ACH depends on provider type and was not confirmed.

NC Medicaid managed-care (Standard/Tailored Plan) negotiated rates — no public fee schedule for ACH services. The PCS increase must be loaded by plans within 45 days and claims reprocessed within 30 days after that [S23].

CAP/DA income limit (sources conflict) and the 2026 CAP/DA slot count after the October 31, 2024 renewal. CAP/DA participants cannot live in an ACH or FCH [S36], so the waiver is not an ACH payer. A secondary agency source reports all 11,648 slots filled [S39].
Number of residents with intellectual or developmental disabilities living in ACHs or FCHs.

BLS OEWS May 2025 NC state-level medians for RN, administrators/managers, cooks and aides — the BLS NC state page was not fetched. Only Raleigh metro group means [S57], the NC all-occupation median [S58], and secondary-site CNA ($18.49/hr) [S59] and LPN ($63,270/yr) [S60] values were found. Wage lines must be labeled accordingly or marked operator estimate.
HUD FY2026 Fair Market Rents for any NC metro and commercial rent benchmarks for adult care home space — not retrieved, so building cost is an operator estimate.

Workers' compensation class-code rate for adult care homes under NCRB 2026 rates — not retrieved; 3+ employee threshold and loss-cost direction (−7.8% average, 4/1/2026 filing) are secondary/official context only [S54][S55].

NC franchise tax applicability to LLCs and any NC entity-level tax — not verified. LLC formation ($125) and annual report ($200 paper / $203 online) figures come from secondary sites citing the Secretary of State [S51][S52][S53].
Production-site confirmation of the 2026-09-25 administrator exam change (online testing only) — the cited page is on a test subdomain [S10].
Enactment status of Senate Bill 863 (streamline ACH inspections) [S22] and any 2026 readoption of 10A NCAC 13F/13G physical-plant rules.

Whether a statutory minimum resident-to-staff ratio applies to a 7–12 bed ACH beyond the verified 'one designated staff per shift' and awake-staff rules for wandering/disoriented residents [S9]. The staffing rule section numbers were not captured; model staffing must be labeled operator estimate beyond those rules.
Several quotes come from search-result excerpts rather than full-page fetches; wording should be rechecked on live pages before publication.

A sourced NC wage for a certified ACH administrator. The model uses the $47,970 all-occupation median as a placeholder owner's draw. The same Commerce deck shows a Management Occupations median of $124,390, and an NC OEWS figure for a comparable occupation (for example 11-9111) was not retrieved, so ACH profit may be overstated. No payroll burden is applied to the administrator.

Who covers the Administrator/Manager requirement for the roughly 128 weekly hours outside a 40-hour administrator under 10A NCAC 13F .0602/.0606. The model assumes every 24/7 aide meets Manager qualifications, and no Manager wage premium or CE cost is priced. Cook and housekeeping coverage for 7-day food service and daily housekeeping by non-care staff is also unverified, and the 12-bed hours may need weekend or relief additions.

The $6,496 NC private-pay median is a secondary-site figure that could not be checked against primary CareScout data. A competing consumer source shows an NC average near $4,586/month, and Genworth 2024 shows $5,769. All private-pay results, break-even figures and net $/month claims inherit this uncertainty, so a sensitivity case at $4,586–$5,769 is recommended.

Raleigh-Cary metro group means for cook ($16.61), housekeeping ($18.92) and activities ($19.29) could not be re-verified (BLS page not retrievable) and are not statewide occupation medians. Statewide OEWS figures for SOC 35-2012, 37-2012 and the activities occupation were not retrieved.

Medicaid PCS revenue per SA resident in an ACH is not modeled. SA residents are automatically Medicaid-eligible and Medicaid helps pay for personal care in an adult care home, so conclusions that SA-heavy mixes lose money apply only to the no-PCS case. Also not verified: the NC UI rate and wage base (DES page not re-fetched), FUTA (not in payroll tax), NC franchise tax, staff TB screening cost, and the 45–60 day SA eligibility lag in working capital.

occupancy.rationale: No North Carolina occupancy rate for adult care homes or family care homes was found in the retrieved sources (see not_claimed). DHSR's licensed-facility listings [S17] were not parsed for it. The 88% default, 80% conservative and 95% optimistic cases are planning assumptions, not sourced NC figures. A 6-bed home swings about 17 points of occupancy per vacancy, so the 80% case matters most there. New homes ramp from a few residents. Verify against local referral flow before committing capital.

payroll_burden.notes: Payroll taxes at 9% = employer FICA 7.65% (federal statutory rate; not in the retrieved source set, so verify) plus North Carolina unemployment tax, which is about 1.4% of a typical full-time aide's pay if the new-employer rate is 1% on the first $34,200 of wages per employee [S48]. The NC UI rate and wage base could not be re-fetched from the DES page and are unverified. Federal FUTA (about 0.6% net on the first $7,000 per employee, roughly $42 per employee per year) is not included in the 9%. Workers' compensation at 4% is an operator estimate: NC requires it at 3+ employees [S54], but the NCRB class-code rate for adult care homes was not retrieved. NCRB loss costs fell an average of 7.8% effective 4/1/2026 [S55], and a further filing is approved effective 4/1/2027 [S56]. Benefits at 5% is an operator estimate. All wages are above the $7.25 NC minimum wage [S49]; no local minimum wage and no scheduled increase [S50]. No payroll burden is applied to the administrator, who is treated as an owner's draw.

sections.executive_summary:
North Carolina has two licensed settings that function as assisted living. The **adult care home (ACH)** has 7 or more licensed residents and is governed by 10A NCAC 13F. The **family care home (FCH)** has 2–6 residents and is governed by 10A NCAC 13G. Both are licensed under G.S. Chapter 131D by the NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation, Adult Care Licensure Section (ACLS) [S1][S2][S3][S5][S13]. NCDHHS reports more than 1,200 adult care homes in the state [S16].

**Market entry is gated.** No one may develop new adult care home beds without a Certificate of Need (CON). CON applications are accepted only for counties where DHSR has scheduled a review, and a decision is due within 150 days of the start of the review period [S1]. CON requirements must be met before a license application is filed for a facility not yet licensed, and licensed bed capacity must match the CON [S3]. In practice, a new 7+ bed operator either wins a CON or buys an existing licensed home, which requires 30 days' written notice of a change of licensee [S3]. Family care homes start at the county DSS adult services section, where the adult home specialist confirms local zoning approval first [S2]. Whether CON applies to 2–6 bed family care homes was not verified.

**Money flows in three ways.** (1) Private pay: CareScout's 2025 North Carolina median for assisted living is $6,496/month ($77,955/yr), against a $6,200 national median. This is a secondary summary of a survey of private one-bedroom units in assisted living communities [S44][S45]. (2) State/County Special Assistance (SA): the facility must accept the state SA rate, which is a maximum of $1,397/month in a regular ACH according to a secondary guide, or $1,792/month in a dementia special care unit. SA is funded 50% state and 50% county, and SA recipients are automatically Medicaid-eligible [S30][S32][S33][S35]. (3) Medicaid personal care services (PCS): NC Medicaid raised the State Plan PCS rate (99509 HA/HB) from $5.96 to $7.03 per unit effective 2026-08-01. Medicaid never pays room and board, and whether an ACH can bill PCS under this code was not confirmed [S23][S35]. The CAP/DA waiver is not an ACH payer, because participants cannot live in an ACH or FCH [S36].

**Bottom line from the model, at the default 88% occupancy:**
- The default configuration, a **20-bed ACH with 75% private pay and 25% Special Assistance**, nets about **$19,823/month** (21.6% margin). It breaks even at about **66.9%** occupancy, first turns profitable in **month 8**, and needs about **$372,475** in cash through ramp-up.
- A **12-bed, 100% private-pay ACH** nets about **$14,844/month** (21.6% margin), breaks even at about **67.3%**, first turns profitable in **month 5**, and needs about **$190,580**.
- A **6-bed, 100% private-pay family care home** nets about **$4,281/month** (12.5% margin), breaks even at about **76.1%**, first turns profitable in **month 6**, and needs about **$92,806**. It needs 5 of its 6 beds filled.
- Mixing Special Assistance into a 6-bed home (4 private + 2 SA) loses about **$4,693/month** and cannot break even at any occupancy (about 106% needed). A **20-bed ACH that is 60% Special Assistance** loses about **$11,586/month** (about 108% needed) when Medicaid PCS is not counted as revenue.

The model does not include the capital cost of a CON, a purchase price or a building, nor debt service. The private-pay price comes from a secondary summary of a survey of private one-bedroom units, not from small shared-room homes, so test it against local comparables before relying on it.

### What this report does not claim
- Which initial license fee governs a new ACH: $400 + $19 per bed on the DHSR page, or the G.S. 131D-2.5 schedule on DHSR forms. The model uses the higher figure.
- CON fees, the 2026/2027 county review schedule, the construction plan-review fee, or whether CON applies to FCHs.
- Statewide bed counts, occupancy, competitor names, market shares, referral-source shares, or SA caseload and waitlist counts. No public source was found.
- How ACHs bill Medicaid PCS, ACH PCS utilization, or negotiated managed-care rates. PCS is not counted as revenue in any configuration.
- Insurance or bond minimums for ACHs and FCHs. None were found; insurance premiums are operator estimates.
- Rent or purchase benchmarks for North Carolina adult care home buildings. Building cost is an operator estimate.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** Adult care homes and family care homes are residential settings for older adults and adults with disabilities who need help with personal care, supervision and medication, but not nursing-home care. The state rules separate the two settings by size. The licensed capacity of an ACH is seven or more residents [S3], and an FCH may have two to six residents [S4][S5]. DHSR's licensing section describes the programs the same way: licensing of adult care homes (seven or more beds) and family care homes (two to six beds) [S13].

**Regulatory framework.**
- *Statute:* G.S. Chapter 131D covers inspection and licensing of both settings [S1][S2][S21].
- *Rulemaking:* the N.C. Medical Care Commission holds rulemaking authority [S1]. The ACH rules are in 10A NCAC 13F [S1][S3] and the FCH rules in 10A NCAC 13G [S2][S4].
- *Regulators:* ACLS licenses and surveys homes. County departments of social services work with DHSR to monitor facilities in their counties at least quarterly [S14].
- *Capacity ties to CON:* an ACH's bed capacity and services must comply with its Certificate of Need [S3].

**Building and site rules scale with size.**
- Family care homes with four to six residents must meet the NC State Building Code, Licensed Residential Care Facilities section [S4].
- ACHs housing seven to twelve residents must meet the Large Residential Care Facilities section [S3].
- Homes of 13 or more residents must meet I-2 Institutional occupancy code for new construction and renovations [S11].
- An ACH must be in a location approved by local zoning boards [S3]. For FCHs the county adult home specialist verifies zoning before the process proceeds [S2].

**Staffing tiers by census** [S9]:
- 7–20 residents: at least one designated staff member per shift for personal care and supervision.
- 7–12 residents: an administrator or manager on site, or within 500 feet with two-way communication, at all times.
- 21–40 residents: 16 aide duty hours on shifts 1 and 2.
- 31 or more residents: a Personal Care Aide Supervisor.
- 81 or more residents: administrator on duty at least eight hours a day, five days a week.

The model's three ACH-type configurations (12 and 20 beds) and two FCH configurations (6 beds) sit inside these tiers. The 20-bed home stays below the 21-resident and 13+ building-code thresholds only on the staffing side. It is above the 13-resident I-2 threshold, which raises capital cost [S11].

**Other programs outside this bundle.** Special Assistance In-Home pays up to the same facility-equivalent amount for people who stay at home [S31][S34]. Special care units for dementia carry a higher SA maximum [S30]. The SCU licensing requirements were not researched, so they are not modeled.
sections.licensing_pathway:
The pathway differs by size. Verify every step with ACLS before spending money, because several fees and one gating question are unresolved (see below).

### Path A — Adult care home (7+ beds), 10A NCAC 13F
1. **Secure beds.** New ACH beds require a Certificate of Need. DHSR accepts applications only for counties with a scheduled review and decides within 150 days of the start of the review period [S1]. The 2026 State Medical Facilities Plan (effective 2026-01-01) governs need, and its Policy LTC-3 covers certification of beds for Special Assistance for applicants proposing new beds under a need determination [S18]. A secondary source says the *Proposed* 2026 plan had adult care need determinations in only two counties, Halifax and Perquimans; the final numbers were not retrieved [S19]. The alternative is buying a licensed home: the current licensee gives written notice to DHSR, county DSS and residents at least 30 days before the change of licensee [S3].
2. **Form the entity.** Online or mail filing for an NC LLC is $125 per a secondary source citing the Secretary of State [S51].
3. **Site and construction review.** Obtain local zoning approval [S3]. DHSR's Construction Section invoices a plan-review fee, and a project is not reviewed until the invoice is paid; the amount is not stated on the pages reviewed [S1]. The building code class depends on size: 7–12 residents Large Residential Care, 13+ I-2 Institutional [S3][S11].
4. **Complete the application packet.** It includes the initial license application (DHSR/AC 4603), a bed capacity statement, plans, the construction review fee, and, on completion, an approved fire and building safety inspection from the local fire marshal plus sanitation and occupancy approvals [S3][S7]. CON requirements must be met *before* the license application is submitted [S3].
5. **Pay the initial fee with the application.** The form states the initial fee must accompany the application [S7]. The DHSR licensing page lists a non-refundable $400 plus $19 per bed (12 beds = $628; 20 beds = $780) [S1]. DHSR forms quoting G.S. 131D-2.5 show a different schedule for homes over six beds ($360 plus $17.50 per bed annually) [S6]. This conflict is unresolved, and the model uses the higher figure. Ask ACLS to confirm the amount in writing.
6. **Pre-licensing survey and decision.** After a survey confirms compliance, ACLS notifies the applicant and county DSS in writing within 14 days of the decision to license or not [S3].
7. **Initial license, then survey.** Initial licenses are issued for six months, after which ACLS must inspect or survey the home [S1].
8. **Renew annually.** Renewal is filed annually on a calendar-year basis with the nonrefundable annual fee [S3]: $360 plus $17.50 per bed, invoiced by ACLS (12 beds = $570; 20 beds = $710) [S1]. ACLS issued a provider memo (P0050, July 23, 2025) on the 2026 renewal application [S15].

### Path B — Family care home (2–6 beds), 10A NCAC 13G
1. **Start with county DSS.** First contact is the adult services section of the local county DSS, not ACLS [S2].
2. **Zoning check.** The adult home specialist verifies the location is approved by the local zoning office before proceeding [S2].
3. **Packet and fee.** The county adult home specialist submits the packet with the $350 licensure fee [S2].
4. **Initial license and first survey.** The initial license runs six months, and a survey is conducted around four months after issuance before a full license [S1][S2].
5. **Renew annually** with the $315 renewal fee on the FCH renewal application [S2]. The statutory fee for homes with six or fewer beds is also $315 [S6].
6. **Background checks.** The state criminal result can take up to about 2 weeks and the FBI check up to 12 weeks [S2].

Whether CON applies to FCHs was not verified. Ask ACLS before committing to a site.

### Administrator certification
ACH administrators must meet G.S. 90-288.14 and be at least 21. The route is a 120-hour Administrator-in-Training program (at least 20 hours of coursework plus at least 100 on-the-job hours), with qualification on education or on 60 months of supervisory experience (or a combination) [S8]. Fees: exam $50, SBI check $14 or $38 with the FBI report, and a $30 renewal with 30 CE hours every two years after the first renewal [S8]. ACLS announced that paper applications and payments for administrator testing end September 25, 2026, in favor of an online test. The cited page is on a test subdomain, so confirm on the production site [S10]. Family care home administrators receive an approval with no renewal fee [S8].

### Other filings
A licensee closing a home gives DHSR, county DSS and residents at least 30 days' notice [S11]. If you enroll as a Medicaid provider, NC charges a $100 application fee on enrollment, re-enrollment and revalidation [S41][S42], and the federal CY2026 institutional fee is $750 [S40]. Which apply to an ACH was not confirmed.
sections.reimbursement:
North Carolina pays for assisted living through three channels, and they behave very differently in the financial model.

### 1. Private pay (the main revenue source in the model)
The CareScout 2025 NC median is $6,496/month ($77,955/yr), from provider-reported rates collected July–November 2025 and published March 2026 (secondary summary) [S44]. The national median is $6,200/month [S45]. An older Genworth 2024 NC figure of $5,769/month is a different survey year and is not comparable [S46]. The survey measures a private one-bedroom unit in an assisted living community. A shared-room 6-bed family care home may price below it.

### 2. State/County Special Assistance (SA)
- SA is the channel for room and board. A facility must agree to accept the state rate for SA residents [S33].
- Rates (2026): a secondary guide lists a maximum charge of $1,397/month in a regular adult care home and $1,792 in a dementia special care unit [S35]. The official SCU brochure confirms $1,792 [S30]. The Enhanced Maintenance Amount is $1,862, which adds the $70 personal needs allowance [S29]. The official SA In-Home basic rate is also $1,397 and the enhanced rate is $1,792 [S31]. The SA In-Home payment is capped at 100% of what the person would receive in an SA facility [S34]. The ACH-specific official table for the regular-home figure was not retrieved.
- The 2026 federal benefit rate that anchors the SA formula is $994/month [S29].
- SA is funded 50% by counties and 50% by the state [S32]. SA beneficiaries are automatically eligible for Medicaid [S32].
- The resident keeps a $70/month personal needs allowance on top of the maximum rate [S31]. It is not facility revenue.
- The model treats $1,397 as the revenue per SA resident-month for a regular ACH or FCH. How that amount splits between the resident's own income and the SA payment was not verified.

### 3. Medicaid personal care services (PCS)
- NC Medicaid applied an 18% increase to current rates for applicable PCS codes effective 2026-08-01. State Plan PCS code 99509 (modifiers HA/HB) moved from $5.96 to $7.03 per unit [S23]. For 99509 with modifiers HC, HH, HI, HQ, SC or TT, the daily per diem is the fee schedule rate times the beneficiary's total pre-approved units [S23].
- The increase is funded by $70.8 million in recurring state funds (S.L. 2026-41, Senate Bill 257, §9E.15) [S23].
- Standard and Tailored Plans have 45 calendar days to load the new rates and 30 more days to reprocess claims back to 2026-08-01 [S23]. One plan said providers could bill $7.03 starting 2026-08-04 [S24]. Fee schedules are posted at ncdhhs.servicenowservices.com/fee_schedules [S23].
- **Medicaid never pays room and board** [S35]. It can help pay for care delivered in a licensed adult care home [S35].
- **Unverified:** how an ACH itself bills PCS (code, modifier or per-diem), the unit length, units per resident, utilization, and the fee-for-service versus managed-care routing. For that reason **no configuration counts PCS as revenue**. If an ACH can bill it, it is upside.

### CAP/DA is not an ACH payer
CAP/DA is a 1915(c) waiver [S37], and participants cannot reside in an ACH or FCH [S36]. NC Medicaid began placing CAP/DA applicants on a waitlist on 2024-02-16, with a capacity of 11,648 slots at the time [S38]. The 2026 slot count after the October 2024 renewal was not retrieved.

### EVV
NC Medicaid's EVV requirement covers in-home PCS under the state plan, 1915(c) waivers and 1115 programs [S25]. Providers should capture EVV data electronically at least 85% of the time, with manual entries kept to 15% or less, and manual entries do not by themselves deny a claim [S26]. NCDHHS selected Sandata as the state aggregator in 2020 [S28]. A vendor page says EVV is not required for adult care homes [S27]; this is unconfirmed on NC Medicaid pages, so ask NC Medicaid before assuming an exemption.

### Cost reporting
Special Assistance and exempt facilities file an Adult Care Cost Report, with the next one due September 30, 2027. For facilities with 7 or more beds, an agreed-upon procedures (AUP) report is no longer required starting on or after July 1, 2026, per S.L. 2026-41 [S47].
sections.demand:
**Population.** NCDHHS's 2025 estimates put the 65-and-older population at 2,038,854, or 18% of the state, projected to reach 2,996,376 (21%) by 2050, an increase of 47%. The 85-and-older population is 186,398 in 2025 and is projected to reach 509,848 by 2050, an increase of 174% [S62]. An earlier NCDHHS plan projected the 65+ population growing from 1.9 million in 2022 to about 2.8 million in 2042 [S63]. About 211,000 North Carolinians aged 65 and older are projected to be living with Alzheimer's in 2025 [S62]. Demand for memory-care capacity is therefore real, though special care unit requirements were not researched.

**Supply is capped by CON, not only by demand.** More than 1,200 adult care homes operate in the state [S16], and DHSR publishes separate ACH and FCH listings updated 07/30/2026 [S17]. New ACH beds can be developed only through CON in counties with a scheduled review [S1]. The final 2026 bed-need numbers by county were not retrieved; a secondary source says the proposed plan had need determinations in only Halifax and Perquimans counties [S19]. One pending project shows the scale of a new build. A CON was filed to relocate 64 memory-care beds from Castle Creek Memory Care to develop The Landings of New Hanover in Wilmington, expected to cost $12.9 million and finish in October 2030 [S20]. That works out to roughly $200,000 per bed (derived). It is a single, memory-care project, not a benchmark for a small conversion. Because bed supply is limited, buying an existing licensed home is often the practical way in.

**Referral flow.** County DSS agencies monitor facilities at least quarterly [S14] and administer Special Assistance [S33], so DSS relationships matter for SA admissions. Referral-source shares (hospital discharge, DSS, family and placement agencies) were not found and are not claimed.

**What waitlists do and do not tell you.**
- The CAP/DA waiver has been waitlisted since 2024-02-16 [S38], and a secondary source says all 11,648 slots are filled [S39]. Waitlists are set county by county [S36]. But CAP/DA participants cannot live in an ACH or FCH [S36], so this waitlist is not an ACH referral pipeline.
- SA In-Home competes for the same SA-eligible people. Enrollment may expand up to 15% of the statewide SA caseload [S34], and a consumer guide says it has had no waitlist since the 2021 cap removal (unverified on a primary page) [S35]. Residents who could otherwise move to an ACH may be supported at home.
- No official waitlist, occupancy or SA caseload figures for ACHs or FCHs were found.
sections.operations:
### Staffing rules to build the schedule around [S9]
- **7–20 residents:** at least one designated staff member per shift to provide personal care and supervision.
- **7–12 residents:** at least one staff member on duty and awake at all times if any resident is disoriented or has wandering behavior. An administrator or manager must be in the facility, or within 500 feet with two-way telecommunication, at all times.
- **21–40 residents:** 16 aide duty hours on the first and second shifts. Third-shift hours vary by census.
- **31 or more:** a Personal Care Aide Supervisor.
- **81 or more:** an administrator on duty at least 8 hours a day, 5 days a week.
- **Manager:** DHSR replaced 'Administrator in Charge' with 'Manager' in the readopted staffing rules effective September 1, 2024. A manager must be 21 or older, hold a high school diploma or GED, and earn 12 hours of CE a year on ACH management or care of the elderly and disabled.
- **CPR:** at least one staff person on the premises at all times must have completed a CPR and choking-management course within the last 24 months [S12].

The 13G family care home staffing rules were not retrieved. The 6-bed model uses one awake aide around the clock (730 hours/month) plus an owner-administrator and a part-time nurse consultant, all labeled operator estimates. Confirm against 10A NCAC 13G before opening.

### Staffing in each model
- **6-bed FCH:** 730 aide hours/month, owner-administrator, and 17.3 nurse-consultant hours/month.
- **12-bed ACH:** 730 awake/manager-qualified hours, a second aide for 486.7 hours (days and evenings), administrator, 34.7 nurse hours, 173.3 cook hours and 86.7 housekeeping hours.
- **20-bed ACH:** 1,216.7 aide hours (above the one-per-shift minimum), administrator, 69.3 nurse hours, a 1.5 FTE cook, one housekeeper and one activities coordinator.

Beyond the verified rules above, hours are operator choices. No statutory resident-to-staff ratio was found for 7–12 residents beyond those rules.

### Administrator
Certification requires the 120-hour AIT program, age 21 or older, and a background check [S8]. Start AIT early, because the administrator must be in place for the pre-licensing survey. The model prices the administrator at the NC all-occupation median wage of $47,970 [S58]. That is a floor, not an NC administrator wage, and it doubles as the owner's draw in owner-operated homes.

### Required systems and compliance
- **Care documentation / eMAR:** modeled at $250/month, an operator estimate.
- **EVV:** applies to in-home PCS [S25]. The statement that ACHs are exempt rests on a vendor page [S27], so confirm before relying on it.
- **Cost report:** SA facilities file the Adult Care Cost Report, next due 2027-09-30 [S47].
- **Star rating and renewals:** DHSR announced rule changes to the N.C. Star Rated Certificate Program effective 2025-08-01 and a memo on the 2026 renewal application [S15]. Watch ACLS announcements [S15].
- **Training budget:** the model carries $150/month for CE, CPR and background checks [S8][S9][S12].

### Employer obligations
- NC unemployment insurance: new-employer rate 1% on the first $34,200 of wages per employee in 2026 [S48].
- Workers' compensation: required for most businesses with three or more employees [S54]. The class-code rate for adult care homes was not retrieved, and the 4% modeled is an operator estimate.
- A secondary guide says E-Verify is mandatory at 25 or more employees [S61]. Part-time staffing in a 20-bed home can approach that count, so check headcount.
- Minimum wage is $7.25, with no local minimum and no scheduled increase [S49][S50]. All modeled wages are well above it.
- The NC LLC annual report is due April 15, $200 paper or $203 online [S52][S53].
sections.market_conditions:
**Pricing.** NC private-pay assisted living is $6,496/month at the CareScout 2025 median, above the $6,200 national median [S44][S45]. Both are secondary summaries. The older Genworth 2024 NC figure of $5,769 is from a different survey year [S46]. None of these measures a shared-room family care home, which may price lower. Special Assistance residents pay far less, at up to $1,397/month in a regular ACH and $1,792 in a special care unit [S30][S35]. The gap between private pay and SA is about $5,099 per resident-month (derived). That spread drives the whole financial model.

**Supply.** More than 1,200 ACHs operate [S16]. New beds require CON in counties with a scheduled review [S1], which limits new entrants and makes existing licensed homes the usual entry point. CON for a project can take years: one pending 64-bed relocation lists a $12.9 million cost and an October 2030 completion [S20]. The 2026 State Medical Facilities Plan took effect 2026-01-01 [S18].

**Wages (May 2025 unless noted).**
- NC all-occupation median: $47,970 per year [S58].
- NC median nursing assistant: $38,460 per year, or $18.49/hour, against $20.32 nationally (secondary, citing BLS OEWS) [S59].
- NC median LPN: $63,270 per year (secondary, citing BLS OEWS) [S60]. The model converts this at 2,080 hours to $30.42/hour.
- Raleigh-Cary group means: food preparation and serving $16.61, building and grounds cleaning and maintenance $18.92, personal care and service $19.29, management $71.52 [S57].

The NC state-level BLS medians for RNs, administrators, cooks and aides were not retrieved. Cook, housekeeping and activities wages in the model use Raleigh metro group means, not statewide occupation medians, so they mix geographies with a statewide private-pay price. They may overstate or understate wages outside the Triangle.

**Cost trends.**
- NC Medicaid raised PCS rates 18% effective 2026-08-01 [S23].
- NCRB workers' compensation loss costs fell an average of 7.8% effective 4/1/2026, and a further filing was approved for 4/1/2027 [S55][S56].
- A 2026 law effective July 1, 2026 directs the Medical Care Commission to amend respite-care rules for ACHs and FCHs as needed [S21].
- Senate Bill 863 (text dated 2026-04-29) proposes to streamline ACH inspections; its enactment status is unverified [S22].

**Not found:** rent or purchase benchmarks for adult care home buildings, HUD fair market rents for NC metros, occupancy rates, and any NC-specific insurance benchmark. Building and insurance costs in the model are operator estimates.
sections.financial_narrative:
### How the model is built
Each configuration computes revenue per resident-month from the rate lines and payer mix, then multiplies by occupied beds. Staffing follows the verified rules plus labeled operator choices, with a payroll burden of 18% (9% payroll taxes, 4% workers' compensation, 5% benefits) [S48][S54]. Rent, utilities base load and maintenance are fixed and sized per licensed bed ($600, $80 and $40 per bed per month), so vacant beds still cost money. DHSR renewal, the LLC annual report, software, accounting, marketing, training, phone/IT and transportation are fixed. Food, per-resident utilities, insurance, supplies and activities scale with census. All per-bed building costs, insurance, supplies and software are **operator estimates — verify locally**, because no NC benchmark was retrieved.

The default occupancy is 88%, with 80% conservative and 95% optimistic. These are planning assumptions, not sourced NC figures, since no NC ACH or FCH occupancy was found.

### Results at 88% occupancy
| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20-bed ACH, 75% private / 25% SA (default) | $19,823 | 21.6% | 66.9% | Month 8 | $372,475 |
| 12-bed ACH, 100% private | $14,844 | 21.6% | 67.3% | Month 5 | $190,580 |
| 6-bed FCH, 100% private | $4,281 | 12.5% | 76.1% | Month 6 | $92,806 |
| 6-bed FCH, 4 private / 2 SA | −$4,693 | −18.5% | 106.3% | Never | $260,727 |
| 20-bed ACH, 40% private / 60% SA | −$11,586 | −19.2% | 107.8% | Never | $817,706 |

Cash needed includes startup costs and the modeled ramp-up deficit. It does **not** include a CON, a purchase price, building acquisition or debt service.

### What drives the result
**1. The private-pay price.** The 20-bed default earns a blended $5,221 per resident-month (75% × $6,496 + 25% × $1,397). Every private resident replaced by an SA resident removes about $5,099 of monthly revenue. Moving the 20-bed home from 25% to 60% SA at 88% occupancy shifts about 6.2 residents and about $31,400 per month, which turns +$19,823 into −$11,586. Costs barely change, because staffing is set by the rules and by operator choice, not by payer.

**2. Whole residents, not percentages.** Break-even occupancy of 76.1% in a 6-bed home is about 4.6 residents. In practice the home needs 5 of 6 beds filled to be in profit, and 4 residents loses money. The 12-bed home needs about 9 residents (67.3% × 12 ≈ 8.1) and the 20-bed default about 14 (66.9% × 20 ≈ 13.4). One discharge matters far more in a small home.

**3. Fixed building cost.** The $600-per-bed rent and per-bed utilities and maintenance are fixed and unsourced. Each $100 per bed per month change in rent moves the 20-bed model by about $2,000/month and the 12-bed by about $1,200 (derived).

**4. Wages.** The administrator is priced at the NC all-occupation median of $47,970 [S58]. This is a floor, not an NC administrator wage. Every $10,000 added to the administrator salary costs roughly $11,800 a year with the 18% burden, about $1,000/month. NC has no local minimum wage above the state's $7.25 [S49][S50], so no metro wage adjustment is needed to stay legal. Aide wages use the NC median nursing assistant wage of $18.49 [S59], while cook, housekeeping and activities wages use Raleigh-Cary group means [S57]. Check wages in your own county.

### Sensitivities (private fee lower than the $6,496 benchmark; costs held constant)
These are derived from the model's resident counts at 88% occupancy, not additional model runs.
- **$500 lower private fee:** the 20-bed default falls by about $6,600/month to about $13,200; the 12-bed by about $5,300 to about $9,500; the 6-bed FCH by about $2,600 to about $1,600.
- **$1,000 lower private fee:** the 20-bed falls to about $6,600 and the 12-bed to about $4,300, and the 6-bed FCH turns negative at about −$1,000/month.
- **Break-even private fee at 88% occupancy:** about $5,685 for the 6-bed FCH, about $5,090 for the 12-bed and about $4,990 for the 20-bed default. The older Genworth 2024 NC figure of $5,769 is not comparable to the CareScout 2025 median [S46] but sits just above the 6-bed break-even. This shows how little cushion the 6-bed model has if its shared-room price lands below the benchmark.
- **Occupancy:** the 6-bed FCH is profitable at 80% occupancy only about 4 points above its 76.1% break-even. At 88% it earns $4,281. Treat the 80% case as the planning case for a 6-bed home.

### What Special Assistance needs to work
At 88% occupancy, the 6-bed FCH with 2 SA residents would need roughly $2,700 more revenue per SA resident-month (about $4,060 total instead of $1,397) just to break even. The 20-bed home with 60% SA would need roughly $1,100 more per SA resident-month (about $2,500 total). Medicaid PCS at $7.03 per unit [S23] is the only verified add-on, and how an ACH bills it, the unit length and the units per resident are all unverified. The model therefore treats PCS as unproven upside and **does not** show these SA-heavy homes as profitable.

### What the model does not include
- CON preparation and fees, purchase price or building acquisition, and debt service. If the operator owns the building, a mortgage replaces the $600-per-bed rent line.
- The DHSR plan-review fee, which DHSR invoices separately [S1].
- Medicaid PCS revenue.
- Income taxes, and any NC franchise tax. The franchise tax line is a $0 placeholder, because applicability was not verified.

### Path to profit
The honest picture is that **private-pay revenue funds the home, and Special Assistance is a minority hedge**. The two profitable multi-resident models (12 and 20 beds) both stay at or below 25% SA. The 12-bed home reaches profit fastest (month 5) and needs the least cash, but it is entirely private-pay and entirely dependent on the $6,496 benchmark holding. The 20-bed default makes more dollars and has more break-even cushion, at about 67% against 88%. It needs a CON or an existing licensed home, I-2 building standards at 13 or more residents [S11], and about twice the cash.
sections.risks:
**Regulatory and market-entry risk**
- *CON:* No new ACH beds without a CON, only in counties with a scheduled review, with a 150-day decision window [S1]. A denied or delayed CON can strand a lease or purchase deposit. Do not sign a lease before the CON or acquisition is certain. The CON application fee and the review schedule were not retrieved.
- *CON for FCHs:* Unverified. Confirm with ACLS before committing to a site.
- *Fee ambiguity:* The initial ACH fee is $400 + $19 per bed on the DHSR page [S1], but the G.S. 131D-2.5 schedule on DHSR forms differs [S6]. Get the amount from ACLS in writing. The plan-review fee is invoiced separately [S1].
- *Rule changes:* The staffing rules were readopted effective 2024-09-01 [S9]. A 2026 law directs respite-care rule amendments [S21], and Senate Bill 863 proposes inspection changes, with enactment unverified [S22]. A star rating program rule change took effect 2025-08-01 [S15].
- *Administrator testing:* The change to online-only testing after 2026-09-25 is confirmed only on a test subdomain [S10].
- *Change of licensee and closure:* Both require 30 days' notice [S3][S11], and a buyer must be licensed before operating.

**Payer risk**
- *Special Assistance cap:* The state sets the maximum facility charge for SA residents, and the home must accept it [S33]. At about $5,099 less per resident-month than private pay, a high SA share turns the models negative (the 20-bed 60% SA home loses about $11,586/month).
- *SA rate source:* The regular-ACH maximum of $1,397 comes from a secondary guide [S35]. Confirm the current amount with your county DSS.
- *County funding:* SA is funded 50% by counties [S32]. County processing and local practice were not researched.
- *PCS:* How ACHs bill PCS was not confirmed. The 18% increase is funded by recurring state appropriations [S23], but plans load rates on a 45-day plus 30-day schedule [S23], and negotiated managed-care rates are not public.
- *SA In-Home diversion:* SAIH pays up to the facility-equivalent rate to people living at home [S31][S34], which may reduce SA referrals to homes.
- *CAP/DA:* Not available to ACH/FCH residents [S36].

**Pricing and census risk**
- The $6,496 median is a secondary summary of a survey of private one-bedroom units [S44]. Small shared-room homes may price lower. At a $1,000 lower fee the 6-bed FCH loses money.
- Small homes swing hard on one vacancy. A 6-bed home needs 5 beds full.
- The 88% default occupancy is an assumption, not an NC figure.

**Cost and staffing risk**
- Rent, utilities, insurance, supplies and software are operator estimates. No NC insurance minimum was found, but lenders and landlords usually require coverage.
- Building class rises with size: 13+ residents must meet I-2 Institutional code for new construction and renovations [S11], which raises capital cost for the 20-bed model.
- Administrator pay is modeled at a floor [S58]. A certified administrator or manager is required at all times in a 7–12 bed home (on site or within 500 feet) [S9].
- Wages use statewide and Raleigh-metro benchmarks that may not match your county [S57][S59].
- Workers' compensation class rates for adult care homes were not retrieved; the 4% is an estimate [S54][S55].

**Compliance risk**
- Failing the CPR/choking requirement (one trained staff member on premises at all times) is a licensing deficiency risk [S12].
- Cost-report filing obligations apply to SA facilities (next due 2027-09-30) [S47].
- EVV status for ACHs is unconfirmed [S25][S27].

**Data limits**
Occupancy, bed counts, SA caseload, waitlists, referral shares, competitor names and market shares were not found in public sources and are not claimed. Several quotes came from search excerpts rather than full-page fetches and should be rechecked on the live pages before publication.
sections.recommendations:
**1. Choose the entry route first, because it decides everything else.** The profitable ACH models assume you already hold licensed beds. Decide between (a) a CON application in a county with a scheduled review (150-day decision; CON before the license application) [S1][S3], or (b) buying an existing licensed home (30 days' notice of change of licensee) [S3]. Check the final 2026 State Medical Facilities Plan for need in your target county before planning around a CON [S18]. For most operators, an acquisition avoids CON risk, but the purchase price and debt service are not in this model, so model them before you sign.

**2. Pick the configuration that matches your capital.**
- *Most robust and highest cash (the default):* a 20-bed ACH with about 75% private pay and 25% Special Assistance. It nets about $19,823/month at 88% occupancy and breaks even at about 66.9%, but needs about $372,475 and reaches profit in month 8.
- *Fastest and leanest ACH:* a 12-bed, all-private ACH. It nets about $14,844/month, breaks even at about 67.3%, reaches profit in month 5, and needs about $190,580. It sits in the Large Residential Care building class (7–12 residents) rather than I-2, which applies at 13 or more [S3][S11].
- *Lowest capital, thinnest margin:* a 6-bed family care home, all private pay and ideally owner-operated. It nets about $4,281/month, breaks even at about 76.1%, and needs about $92,806. It works only if you hold 5 of 6 beds and can price at or near the benchmark.

**3. Cap Special Assistance at about one quarter of beds, and do not take it in a 6-bed home.** The SA-heavy models both lose money at 88% occupancy [S35]. Mixing 2 SA residents into a 6-bed home loses about $4,693/month. If you take SA residents, do it deliberately, in a larger home with a private-pay base. Before counting any Medicaid PCS, ask NC Medicaid and the managed-care plans whether and how an ACH bills it, in what units, and at what volume [S23].

**4. Test your price before you commit.** Gather three to five local comparables for shared and private rooms, and compare them with the $6,496 CareScout median [S44]. If your achievable fee is below about $5,700, the 6-bed FCH does not work, and below about $5,100 the 12-bed does not. Use the break-even fees in the financial narrative as your go/no-go line.

**5. Run the licensing sequence in order.**
1. Form the LLC [S51].
2. Confirm local zoning (and, for an FCH, start with the county DSS adult home specialist) [S2][S3].
3. Obtain CON or complete acquisition steps [S1][S3].
4. Pay the DHSR plan-review invoice and complete construction review, then fire, sanitation and occupancy approvals [S1][S3].
5. Submit the application with the initial fee [S7], and confirm the fee amount with ACLS in writing.
6. Pass the pre-licensing survey and receive the six-month initial license [S1][S3].
7. Calendar the follow-up survey, with an FCH survey about four months after the initial license [S2].

**6. Get the administrator started early.** Enroll in the 120-hour AIT program, complete the background check (the FBI check can take up to 12 weeks) and take the online exam [S2][S8][S10]. Confirm the testing change on the production DHSR site.

**7. Staff to the rules, then to your census.** Meet the awake-staff, manager-within-500-feet and one-designated-staff-per-shift rules for 7–12 residents [S9]. Keep the 20-bed home under the 21-resident aide-hour tier unless the extra residents justify the added hours [S9]. Keep one CPR-trained person on premises at all times [S12]. Confirm 10A NCAC 13G staffing before finalizing an FCH schedule.

**8. Resolve the open items before you spend.**
- Ask ACLS: the initial fee, whether CON applies to a 2–6 bed home, and any 2026 changes to the physical-plant rules.
- Ask your county DSS: current SA maximum, referral process and payment timing.
- Ask your insurance broker for a quote, since no minimum was found in the rules reviewed.
- Ask a CPA: franchise tax applicability and entity structure.
- Ask NC Medicaid: enrollment fees by provider type, EVV status and PCS billing for ACHs.

**9. Plan cash for the ramp.** The cash figures include ramp-up deficits: $92,806, $190,580 and $372,475 for the three profitable models. Add the CON or purchase cost, plan-review fee and a cushion beyond the modeled 3–6 month working capital. Do not open without that reserve.

checklist.task: Choose your license category: Family Care Home (2–6 beds) or Adult Care Home (7+ beds)
checklist.instructions: NC licenses two categories through DHSR's Adult Care Licensure Section (ACLS). A family care home (FCH) has 2–6 residents and falls under 10A NCAC 13G. An adult care home (ACH) has 7 or more residents and falls under 10A NCAC 13F. Both are licensed under G.S. Chapter 131D. Your choice sets the entry route (county DSS for an FCH, CON for new ACH beds), the building code, the staffing rules and the fees.

checklist.task: Review the bundle financial model and pick a configuration that clears break-even
checklist.instructions: Open the Pro Forma P&L. At the default occupancy the model shows: 20-bed ACH at 75% private pay / 25% Special Assistance, net about $19,823/month, break-even occupancy 66.9%, first profit month 8, cash needed about $372,475. 12-bed ACH at 100% private pay, net about $14,844/month, break-even 67.3%, first profit month 5, cash needed about $190,580. 6-bed FCH at 100% private pay, net about $4,281/month, break-even 76.1%, first profit month 6, cash needed about $92,806. The 6-bed FCH with 2 Special Assistance residents and the 20-bed ACH at 60% Special Assistance both lose money in the model. Replace the operator-estimate lines (rent, utilities, insurance) with local quotes before committing capital.

checklist.task: Decide your payer mix and whether you will accept State/County Special Assistance (SA) residents
checklist.instructions: A facility must agree to accept the state SA rate to receive SA residents. The 2026 SA maximum is $1,397/month in a regular ACH (secondary guide, matching the official SA-In-Home basic rate) and $1,792/month in a special care unit. The resident keeps a $70 personal needs allowance on top. SA is funded 50% state and 50% county, and SA recipients are automatically eligible for Medicaid. Medicaid never pays room and board. Heavy SA mixes lose money in this model, so cap SA beds to what your fixed costs can absorb.

checklist.task: Decide whether to serve memory-care (Alzheimer's/dementia) residents in a special care unit
checklist.instructions: SA pays a higher room-and-board cap in an ACH special care unit: $1,792/month in 2026, with an Enhanced Maintenance Amount of $1,862 that includes the $70 allowance. The 2026 SMFP Policy LTC-3 covers certification of beds for Special Assistance. The special care unit licensing and construction requirements were not researched for this bundle, so ask ACLS before you design the building. About 211,000 North Carolinians 65+ are projected to live with Alzheimer's in 2025.
